mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes GLC63 AMG engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rebuilt M177 V8 engine for the GLC63 costs £7,000-£14,000 supply-only; a rebuilt M139l PHEV four-cylinder costs £9,000-£15,000 supply-only. Fitting adds £1,500-£2,500 depending on complexity - AMG V8 and PHEV work requires specialist knowledge.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of oil separator failure on a Mercedes GLC63?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most common sign is a burning oil smell or oil dripping from the rear of the engine. A simple test - attempting to remove the oil fill cap at idle - can reveal excessive vacuum (cap difficult to remove) or excessive pressure (air release). If ignored, oil separator failure leads to rear main seal leaks and potential engine damage.

mainEntity.name: Is the Mercedes GLC63 V8 engine reliable?

acceptedAnswer.text: The M177 is a fundamentally strong hand-built AMG V8 - one of Mercedes' most impressive modern engines. It has a small number of well-documented weak points (oil separator, rear main seal, turbochargers) that are well understood by specialists. With proper maintenance, the M177 routinely exceeds 100,000 miles.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Mercedes GLC63 engine last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Properly maintained M177 V8 engines routinely reach 100,000-150,000 miles before major work. The M139l PHEV four-cylinder is too new for definitive long-term data - reliability is unproven as of 2026.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in my Mercedes GLC63?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the GLC63 is otherwise in good condition with no rust or major electrical faults. A rebuilt M177 costs £7,000-£14,000 - far less than replacing a £35,000-£60,000 vehicle. The GLC63's strong residual values make engine replacement financially justifiable.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between the V8 GLC63 and the new PHEV GLC63?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 2017-2022 GLC63 uses the M177 4.0L twin-turbo V8 (476-510hp) with a characterful AMG soundtrack. The 2024-present GLC63 S E Performance uses the M139l 2.0L four-cylinder with plug-in hybrid (671hp) - more power, but a very different character. The V8 has been discontinued; the new model is a completely different car.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes Benz GLC Class GLC63 - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The GLC63 AMG launched in 2017 as the flagship performance variant of the X253 GLC range. Powered by the hand-built M177 4.0-litre twin-turbo V8 - shared with the C63 and AMG GT - it held the title of the world's fastest SUV when it went on sale. In 2024, the second-generation X254 GLC63 replaced the V8 with a 2.0-litre four-cylinder plug-in hybrid producing 671hp - more power, but a very different character.

milestones.description: Facelift X253/C253; M177 continues with 476hp and 510hp outputs unchanged
X253 GLC63 production ends; V8 discontinued
M139l PHEV, 2.0L four-cylinder with plug-in hybrid, 671hp (X254 GLC63 S E Performance)

commonProblems.h2: Mercedes Benz GLC Class GLC63 Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The GLC63's M177 twin-turbo V8 is one of AMG's most impressive modern engines - a hand-built masterpiece that delivers serious power and performance. However, as these vehicles accumulate mileage, a small number of well-documented issues can drive significant repair costs. The most frequent and expensive problem is oil separator failure, which often leads to rear main seal leaks. Every rebuilt engine supplied through EnginesMarket includes upgraded components addressing the original failure point, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.group: M177 Oil Separator Failure & Rear Main Seal Leak
problems.h4: M177 Oil Separator Failure & Rear Main Seal Leak - The Most Expensive M177 Problem
problems.rootCause: The oil separator (part of the crankcase ventilation system) fails, causing unbalanced crankcase pressure. Excessive positive pressure forces oil past engine seals, or excessive negative pressure (vacuum) pulls seals inward, distorting them. The rear main seal - sitting at the back of the crankshaft where the engine meets the transmission - is often the first to fail. Symptoms include oil dripping from the rear of the engine, oil around the transmission bellhousing, or a burning oil smell.

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical 2017-2022 GLC63 AMG 4MATIC+ is worth approximately £35,000-£60,000 depending on mileage and condition. The GLC63 sits firmly in the £15,000+ band - replacement cost is typically small relative to vehicle value, making a full rebuilt engine a justifiable investment for owners of these high-value performance SUVs.
problems.recommendation: The oil separator is the root cause of most M177 rear main seal leaks. If you notice oil around the transmission bellhousing or a burning oil smell, have the crankcase pressure checked immediately. A simple test - attempting to remove the oil fill cap at idle - can reveal excessive vacuum (cap difficult to remove) or excessive pressure (air release). If caught early, replacing the oil separator alone (£500-£800 at a specialist) prevents the much more expensive rear main seal replacement. If the rear main seal has already failed, replacing both the seal and the oil separator together is the only sensible approach. On a GLC63 worth £35,000-£60,000, the full rebuilt engine route is justifiable if bottom-end damage has occurred.

problems.group: M177 Ignition Coil & Fuel Injector Issues
problems.h4: M177 Ignition Coil & Fuel Injector Issues - Misfire and Check Engine Light
problems.rootCause: The M177 can suffer from ignition coil failures and fuel injector leakage, causing misfires and check engine lights. Raw fuel can damage catalytic converters if not addressed promptly.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace faulty ignition coil(s), inspect spark plugs
Replace faulty fuel injector(s), clean or replace affected spark plugs
Supply & fit rebuilt M177 engine with new injectors and coils
repairOptions.longevity: If raw fuel has damaged catalytic converters or bores

problems.vehicleValueCheck: As above - a typical GLC63 is worth £35,000-£60,000.
problems.recommendation: Ignition coil and fuel injector issues on the M177 are usually straightforward to diagnose and repair. If you experience a misfire or check engine light, have a specialist perform a cylinder contribution test and fuel trim analysis. Replace ignition coils in pairs or as a full set to avoid repeat failures. If fuel injector leakage is confirmed, replace the affected injector(s) and change the engine oil and spark plugs immediately. Ignoring fuel injector leakage can lead to catalytic converter damage and, in extreme cases, bore wash and cylinder scoring - at which point a full engine replacement becomes the only option.

problems.h4: M177 Turbocharger Failure - Oil Starvation and High Temperatures
problems.rootCause: The M177's twin-scroll turbochargers are mounted in the hot-vee configuration, subjecting them to high temperatures. Oil starvation, often caused by oil separator failure or neglected oil changes, can lead to turbocharger bearing failure.

problems.recommendation: Preventative maintenance is the key to avoiding M177 turbocharger failure. Use only Mercedes-spec oil (MB 229.5) and change it every 10,000 miles or 12 months - never stretch the interval. If you hear a high-pitched whistle, notice a loss of power, or see blue smoke from the exhaust, have the turbochargers inspected immediately. If one turbo has failed, replace both - the other will typically fail within a short period due to shared oil supply and similar operating conditions.
